As mentioned in § E.3, consider Write(k,7)(k,7) for an initially absent key. All replicas accept the write, but their acceptance replies to the leader are delayed, so the leader has not committed it or replied to the writing client. A responder nevertheless receives enough accept notifications to return 77 to a read. After that read completes, a second read reaches the leader, which returns absence from its unchanged committed state. Returning 77 and then absence in two successive reads violates linearizability.

Duplicate writes after timeout retries.

The client-side timeout retry path in Bodega [29]’s implementation assigns a new request identifier to each attempt, so the server can execute the original request and its retry as separate writes. As mentioned in § E.4, consider a write that sets x=1x=1 but whose reply is delayed. Another client reads 11 and then completes a write of 22. After a timeout, the original client retries with a new identifier; the retry sets x=1x=1 again, and a later read returns 11. If both attempts represent one client write, the first read requires that write to precede the write of 22, so the final read must return 22. This violates linearizability even though replicas agree on the order of the individual requests.

9 Related Work

State-machine replication.

Paxos supplies the ballot-and-quorum safety baseline for replicated agreement [38]. FastPaxos then lets proposers send values directly to acceptors in prepared fast rounds, enabling two-message-delay learning without collisions at the cost of stronger quorum intersection and recovery rules [40]. Later systems remove different parts of the consensus critical path. Mencius spreads log slots across rotating coordinators [48]. EPaxos and Atlas use per-command coordination and dependency ordering, and Atlas additionally sizes its fast quorum around a chosen concurrent site-failure budget [49, 20]. Rabia uses randomized weak multi-valued consensus to avoid a distinguished leader and separate fail-over protocol [58]. Later analysis exposed EPaxos’s tail-latency and recovery subtleties [75], while SwiftPaxos reduces the cost of dependency disagreement through leader-including quorums and double voting [63].

Other designs change the system boundary or optimize a particular workload. NOPaxos and Hydra move common-case ordering into the network [41, 15]. CURP uses witnesses for unordered durability when operations commute [59], and Jetpack retrofits a parallel one-RTT path onto compatible consensus protocols [72]. Copilot tolerates one slow replica by redundantly processing commands at two pilots [52]. Bodega combines roster leases with responder-covering write quorums for local linearizable reads during interfering writes [29].

AI-driven algorithm and systems discovery.

AlphaEvolve combines LLM-driven evolutionary search with automated evaluators to discover improved algorithms [54]. ADRS studies this approach in systems research, using OpenEvolve [67], an open-source framework inspired by AlphaEvolve, for tasks such as spot-instance scheduling, mixture-of-experts load balancing, and transaction scheduling [14]. Glia instead uses a multi-agent LLM workflow, in which a researcher agent proposes, implements, and evaluates designs in a simulator under a supervisor agent, to design request-routing, scheduling, and autoscaling policies for LLM-serving clusters [24]. These frameworks optimize isolated policies in which every candidate is valid by construction or checked exactly, and a simulator scores it in seconds. ADRS identifies consensus protocols, whose logic spans state management, communication, and failure handling, as a poor fit for this approach. AI-greement targets this gap, where three challenges arise together: (C1) faster candidates can break safety, (C2) tests cannot establish safety, and (C3) each candidate takes minutes to hours to evaluate. Table 4 and Table 6 in Appendix F compare these approaches and the challenges they face.

Agent-synthesized verified systems.

The SkyDiscover framework [44], from the authors of ADRS, extends this line from evolving isolated programs to synthesizing complete systems. Its proof-driven mode, IDS [2], is the work closest to AI-greement: agents jointly synthesize an implementation and its Rocq proof, use incomplete proofs as a search oracle, and use benchmarks to steer toward efficient designs, producing verified distributed key-value stores for session and causal consistency specifications. IDS, however, starts from a fixed, human-written specification, so performance only ranks candidates that already meet it (sidestepping C1), and its design freedom lies in data layout and proof structure rather than in new protocol mechanisms. Its targets involve neither fault-tolerant agreement nor recovery. AI-greement instead designs new consensus protocols under a performance objective. Conversely, IDS proves the extracted implementation, whereas our Lean proofs cover a protocol model whose correspondence to the prototype is additionally checked by a human consensus expert.

AI for consensus.

Prior AI work on consensus finds bugs in existing protocols, generates small protocols, or assists human protocol designers. Agora’s agents inspect Raft, EPaxos, HotStuff, and BullShark codebases, synthesize attacks, and generate executable tests. Agora reports 15 new defects classified as protocol-level logic bugs because the observed executions violate protocol properties [45]. GGMS learns protocols without an LLM, combining Monte Carlo tree search, a transformer action encoder, and a model checker [32]. It targets synchronous consensus and atomic commit with crash failures, and verifies candidates by exhaustive model checking for at most four processes. For consensus, it rediscovers FloodSet [46]. By dropping the performance objective and restricting the search to four processes, it sidesteps C1 and keeps evaluation cheap (C3), but its guarantees do not extend beyond the checked instance sizes. An LLM also substantially assisted the design and proofs of a communication-efficient Byzantine broadcast protocol [19]. There, however, humans drive an interactive collaboration toward an asymptotic bound established by pen-and-paper proof; no candidate is implemented or measured, so C3 does not arise and safety checking (C2) rests on the authors. AI-greement instead faces all three challenges: it designs protocols under a latency objective and evaluates them on deployments of up to 17 replicas.

10 Conclusion: The End of Consensus Research?

Our answer is no; this is just a new beginning. We believe this work marks a turning point in how consensus research is conducted. The low latency achieved might still be decreased in specific situations we did not focus on. More generally, our consensus solution could be extended to other failure models and settings. Our results show that AI agents can take on substantial parts of the research process, including retrieving protocol knowledge, designing and implementing candidates, as well as constructing formal arguments and counterexamples. Human expertise, however, remains essential for defining performance objectives and safety requirements, designing evaluation environments, and reviewing agent behavior and research outcomes. A crucial question therefore is: how do our results reshape the role of consensus researchers?

10.1 Where Is Human Judgment Needed?

From our experiences, we found that human judgment was needed before, during, and after the agentic search.

Before the search.

Human expertise is required before the quest starts. Researchers need to develop the agent harness by checking the protocol knowledge base, defining the implementation interfaces, and choosing the fault model, correctness properties, performance objectives, and evaluation conditions (§ 3). Although an agent drafted the knowledge-base notes, we verified them against the source papers and corrected errors. This preparation determines which designs the agent can express and what its feedback measures.

During the search.

Inspecting an agentic run while it is in progress allows researchers to steer the agent early and avoids restarting a long run that wastes many tokens. Giving the agent an explicit budget, such as a fixed amount of time to search for a new candidate, can reduce the need for such manual checks.

After the search.

Human review remains necessary when interpreting improvements. As described in § 6, the agent duplicated requests over two TCP connections to the same destination to exploit independently sampled network jitter. The resulting latency reduction reflected an opportunity in the benchmark’s delay model, and we removed the mechanism before the final evaluation. A separate test set helps expose overfitting, but shared assumptions in the development and test environments can still reward such shortcuts. Researchers must therefore examine both candidate protocols and their evaluation environments to reduce the risk of reward hacking.

Human review can also expose inefficiencies that the agent’s own tuning left in place. In A-greement’s batching (§ 5.1), the leader cuts a batch into log entries in arrival order. This couples some writes to the slower completion of a hot key and fragments batches when completion owners alternate. Grouping each batch by completion owner would remove both inefficiencies and is safe, but the agent chose not to do it. Moreover, upon a ballot change A-greement does not restore the cold quorum (§ 4.5), moving all write-related actions to the common log, essentially sacrificing a part of its optimization for no reason. We did not fix either of these inefficiencies, so that the evaluated protocol stays as close as possible to the agent’s design, with only correctness-critical fixes.

Human review is also necessary for formal verification. Lean checks proofs against the encoded specification; researchers must check that this specification faithfully captures the protocol and its implementation. In our experience, formalizing a protocol from pseudocode presents substantially different challenges from formalizing it from implementation code. The discovery loop could generate an implementation first and then formalize its behavior, or develop both the implementation and the formal specification from shared pseudocode. Which approach produces more faithful specifications with less human intervention remains an open question.

10.2 The Changing Role of Researchers

As agents take on more research tasks, we believe that human researchers retain three central responsibilities. First, they must define meaningful problems and translate practical requirements into explicit research objectives. This includes deciding which workloads and deployment conditions matter, what safety and availability guarantees are required, and how to prioritize latency, throughput, and resource costs. These decisions give the agent a concrete target and determine which tradeoffs are acceptable. Second, they must test and review agent outputs, which may still contain hallucinations, implementation errors, or unsupported conclusions. Generated code, explanations, and experimental reports require independent scrutiny before they can support a research claim. Researchers must assess whether the evidence justifies the claimed improvement, investigate failures and unexpected behavior, and determine how broadly the conclusions apply. Third, they remain important for proposing new ideas and opening directions beyond the current search. The search reported here primarily combined and adapted known mechanisms, showing how agents can explore combinations that are costly to investigate manually. Human researchers can contribute new abstractions, question assumptions inherited from existing protocols, and formulate hypotheses that expand the design space. Agents can then help develop these ideas into protocols, construct implementations and proofs, and evaluate their consequences, allowing researchers to pursue more alternatives and refine the ideas using concrete evidence.

Appendix A Detailed A-greement Specification

This appendix specifies the three write paths introduced in § 4: completion at a designated replica, direct client learning from the ordinary log, and direct client learning from the cold per-key history. The first two paths share log state and recovery. We specify their different completion and read-visibility rules explicitly. Message names below describe logical actions; transport framing, compression, and retransmission do not change the evidence required by a handler.

A.1 State, Identity, and Authority

Requests and retained state.

A request cc contains an identifier id⁡(c)\operatorname{id}(c), its operation, key, and original payload. Retries preserve this identity and command body. An ordinary request also retains its designated reply replica. This identity is needed to determine whether the completion owner controls the request’s reply. The cold fast path completes at the client and has no completion-owner role. Participants are non-Byzantine. Vote sets count distinct replica identities; hashes bind content and are not signatures. We assume that different retained bodies do not collide under the content hash HH.

Ordinary state.

Ballot bb installs leader LbL_{b} and responder sets Sb​(k)S_{b}(k). Slot ss contains an ordered batch E=(b,s,C,𝑓𝑟𝑒𝑠ℎ)E=(b,s,C,\mathit{fresh}); CC includes the original requests and their logical reply destinations. A fresh entry was newly proposed in the current ballot; a recovered entry is not fresh. Replicas retain accepted entries, votes, completion identifiers, and the highest contiguous executed slot executedPrefix. The completion-owner assignment, when applicable, is denoted Ob​(k)O_{b}(k); a delegated owner must remain an authorized responder. Otherwise, the leader supplies the default owner used by the read shortcut. The ordinary executed-reply route still follows the request’s retained reply destination.

For a batch, define its required reader coverage as

Sb(E)=⋃c∈C:op⁡(c)=WriteSb(key(c)).S_{b}(E)=\bigcup_{c\in C:\,\operatorname{op}(c)=\textsc{Write}}S_{b}(\operatorname{key}(c)).

An ordinary completion certificate contains matching acceptance evidence V⁡(E)V(E) satisfying |V⁡(E)|≥m|V(E)|\geq m and Sb​(E)⊆V​(E)S_{b}(E)\subseteq V(E). A Paxos majority fixes the log value; responder coverage is the additional condition used here before completion or exposure of a not-yet-executed value. Below, an ordinary entry marked covered-chosen satisfies both conditions. A trusted current-ballot commit notification can convey this outcome, but it does not supply a missing batch body or authorize reading a different ballot’s entry.

For a fresh current-ballot entry EE, a gate candidate is a non-certificate write whose designated reply replica is its completion owner. If the candidates in EE all name the same owner pp, define the completion gate g⁡(E)=pg(E)=p; if there is no candidate or candidates name different owners, let g(E)=⊥g(E)=\bot. Normal batching splits entries when candidate ownership changes, and an unsplit conflicting entry conservatively has no gate. A local acceptance counts in V⁡(E)V(E) immediately, but g⁡(E)g(E) does not publish its Accepted or any client vote for the entry until it has itself marked EE covered-chosen. Thus the gate advances its read target before its vote can allow another learner to complete the entry.

Cold state.

Cold control state has generation G=(b,e)G=(b,e), where ee is an epoch within ballot bb. Epochs distinguish freeze and resume barriers, including those used by scans. Each key also has a key-round number aa. Rounds (b,e,a)(b,e,a) are ordered lexicographically; version vv identifies the position in the key’s history, independently of its round. A cold vote binds

(b,e,a,k,v,id⁡(c),H⁡(c),replyTo⁡(c),timestamp⁡(c),Qb).(b,e,a,k,v,\operatorname{id}(c),H(c),\operatorname{replyTo}(c),\operatorname{timestamp}(c),Q_{b}).

Here H⁡(c)H(c) hashes the original operation, key, and payload; the remaining fields bind its request and routing identity. The fast quorum QbQ_{b} has size mm and remains fixed across key rounds and scan epochs within an installed ballot. A new ballot may select a different quorum for recovery. For each key, a replica retains its promise, chosen prefix, accepted tail, chosen evidence, pending original requests, duplicate identifiers, and readiness state. A bare payload or routing hint supplies none of this authority.

Lease and installation preconditions.

Local reads require an installed roster and a majority of unexpired lease grants whose catch-up thresholds the responder has executed. Self-grants count only when the local threshold is met. A leader must additionally have completed ordinary preparation. Grantor and holder deadlines include a conservative clock-drift margin; delayed renewal replies cannot restore a revoked ballot. Before replacing conflicting read authority, grantors revoke the old grants and receive acknowledgments, or wait until the grants expire. Failure suspicion starts this process but cannot replace it. Cold readers also require the installed generation to equal the promised generation and the key to be ready.

Completion policy.

Let η\eta be the measured hot boundary and τ≥η\tau\geq\eta the selected cold boundary, defined in § A.7. Under the reference policy, fresh ordinary writes to observed ranks below η\eta complete through their reply destination after execution; ranks at or above η\eta are eligible for direct certificates unless routed to the cold path. The alternative policy enables direct certificates for all ordinary keys, including hot and unobserved keys. Unobserved keys never enter the cold path. Recovered entries are ineligible for early ordinary completion, and bridge acceptance disables new early votes. Thus heat classification, completion-owner placement, and certificate eligibility are related planning decisions, not interchangeable definitions.

A.2 Normal-Operation Details

Ordinary read visibility.

Each Accepted vote reports acceptedPrefix, the highest slot through which the sender has accepted a contiguous current-ballot sequence. The mmth largest report, counting missing reports as zero, is majorityFixedPrefix. It fixes the preceding entry identities and the first occurrences of duplicate request identifiers; it does not establish responder coverage by itself.

The target of a read depends on whether its responder gates completion. At replica pp, let Ap​(k)A_{p}(k) be the greatest accepted slot touching kk, Cp​(k)C_{p}(k) the greatest covered-chosen slot touching kk, and Dp​(k)D_{p}(k) the greatest accepted slot touching kk for which the write is not a gate candidate for pp or g⁡(E)≠pg(E)\neq p. Missing positions are zero. Direct-certificate writes, writes with another reply destination, recovered entries, different-ballot entries, and entries without a unique gate therefore contribute to Dp​(k)D_{p}(k). The read target is

tp​(k)={max⁡{Cp​(k),Dp​(k)},p=Ob​(k),Ap​(k),otherwise.t_{p}(k)=\begin{cases}\max\{C_{p}(k),D_{p}(k)\},&p=O_{b}(k),\\ A_{p}(k),&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

The gate can therefore bypass its gated pending entries while its vote remains unpublished: no other learner can yet establish responder coverage. It cannot bypass an accepted entry without this gate. After collecting majority and coverage evidence, it marks the entry covered-chosen and advances Cp​(k)C_{p}(k) before releasing its vote; subsequent reads target the chosen write.

After checking read authority, a responder returns applied state if tp​(k)≤executedPrefixt_{p}(k)\leq\texttt{executedPrefix}. Otherwise, it can return the last write to kk in that slot only when the entry is covered-chosen, fresh, in the current ballot, and within majorityFixedPrefix. This reads a chosen value without executing an arbitrary log suffix. If any required condition is missing, the read waits. strictPrefix disables this shortcut after handoff. No read may bypass an unapplied bridge. Authority and visibility are rechecked when a waiting read is released.

Cold fast-path details.

Each cold key advances through versions vv in order. The round (b,e,a)(b,e,a) distinguishes voting authority from version order; the leader coordinates preparation and conflict recovery. The client sends its original write in ColdPropose to all of QbQ_{b} and sends Intent to notify the coordinator of the pending write. Acceptors require the installed, prepared generation and a fast-enabled key round. Each proposes its locally next version v=keyPrefix​(k)+1v=\texttt{keyPrefix}(k)+1; differing prefixes cannot produce matching votes. They retain the full command, block local reads of the key, and send FastVote directly to the client. Within (b,e,a,k,v)(b,e,a,k,v), they vote for only one command; retries repeat that vote. Each vote binds the ballot, epoch, key round, key, version, request identifier, command digest, original reply destination, client timestamp, and fixed quorum. Matching FastVotes from all of QbQ_{b} form the fast certificate, completing the write. The client asynchronously disseminates this certificate as a ChosenProof. Identical retries of chosen requests may receive ColdDone, binding the original identifier, key, and digest. Replicas execute in per-key order, fetching missing proofs or bodies while retaining pending commands.

Each round permits exactly one fast quorum, reducing Fast Paxos’s recovery-intersection requirement [40] to

P∩Qb≠∅for every majority ​P.P\cap Q_{b}\neq\varnothing\qquad\text{for every majority }P.

Only the designated quorum can vote in a fast round. A member’s failure blocks this path and triggers roster recovery.

Collision fallback and cold reads.

Competing writes trigger a higher key round. The coordinator collects complete snapshots from a majority and preserves chosen prefixes and tails that might already have been chosen. It then enters a classic round, proposing one safe value for replica acceptance. The value requires matching votes from every member of QbQ_{b}. Losing inputs remain pending for later versions. Fast resumption requires a higher prepare, a safe empty remaining tail, and catch-up and Ready replies from all of QbQ_{b} confirming installation of the prepared key round.

Cold reads require caught-up members of the installed QbQ_{b} and leases from the parent roster. The predicate keyReady(k) records installation and catch-up of the chosen key prefix in the prepared round. An unresolved accepted tail blocks reads until a valid chosen prefix is installed. Completed fast writes fence all cold readers, even before proof delivery; neither routing hints nor payloads restore reads.

A.3 Leader and Cold-Plane Recovery

Leadership change and ordinary recovery.

Failure suspicion triggers a higher-ballot leader or replacement of an unavailable required read responder; suspicion alone cannot select values or authorize reads. Replicas suspend old read authority, revoke grants or await expiration, and retain accepted evidence. The new leader runs Paxos phase one: it sends Prepare, collects complete promises from mm replicas, and adopts the highest-ballot accepted entry at each remaining log slot. Only unreported gaps receive internal no-ops. It re-accepts recovered entries under the new roster with 𝑓𝑟𝑒𝑠ℎ\mathit{fresh} cleared. New read responders require majority grants and catch-up through reported thresholds.

Recovering possible cold choices.

The coordinator sends ColdPrepare for a frozen generation G′=(b′,e′)G^{\prime}=(b^{\prime},e^{\prime}) with b′>bb^{\prime}>b to freeze the cold plane: replicas stop old cold-path votes and promise G′G^{\prime} over all admitted cold keys and their future versions. A majority PP returns PromiseCatalog replies containing complete immutable catalogs of chosen prefixes, duplicate identifiers, accepted tails, historical ballots, key rounds, quorums, and references to command bodies.

For an open version, recovery first selects the highest reported accepted round (b0,e0,a)(b_{0},e_{0},a), ordered lexicographically. Classic rounds retain their unique accepted value. Fast rounds using Qb0Q_{b_{0}} retain xx if

∀p∈P∩Qb0:p reports acceptance of x at (b0,e0,a).\forall p\in P\cap Q_{b_{0}}:\quad p\text{ reports acceptance of }x\text{ at }(b_{0},e_{0},a).

This condition identifies a possible old fast choice, not a new certificate. Because |P|=|Qb0|=m|P|=|Q_{b_{0}}|=m and |R|=2​f+1|R|=2f+1, the intersection is nonempty. Any value previously accepted by all of Qb0Q_{b_{0}} must appear at every member of this intersection, provided each promise is complete. A missing acceptance in a complete snapshot rules out that candidate; a missing snapshot or body does not. Recovery uses the identities of intersecting replicas, not just a count of matching reports. If no value could have been fast-chosen, the coordinator deterministically selects a retained original input and leaves others pending. It records recovered prefixes, selected tails, and body references in a manifest that remains immutable for generation G′G^{\prime}. Missing bodies must be fetched from original holders; their absence cannot justify discarding a possible choice.

Recovered state and its certificate.

The frozen manifest M=(G′,Qb′,…)M=(G^{\prime},Q_{b^{\prime}},\ldots) records recovered prefixes, chosen identifiers, and selected classic tails. Together, these form the foundation state to be transferred into the ordinary log. The coordinator broadcasts MM and H⁡(M)H(M) in BulkAccept. Each BulkVote requires a matching promise, local retention of every referenced body, installation of valid chosen-prefix evidence, and acceptance of every selected tail. Matching voters VMV_{M} must satisfy |VM|≥m|V_{M}|\geq m and Qb′⊆VMQ_{b^{\prime}}\subseteq V_{M}; Qb′Q_{b^{\prime}} is selected from complete promise respondents. BulkCommit certifies the tails for per-key application. Replicas acknowledge application with BulkApplied. All of Qb′Q_{b^{\prime}} and the coordinator must finish application; Ready replies from all of Qb′Q_{b^{\prime}} confirm installation before the log transition is proposed. Bulk recovery shares evidence transfer across keys.

One-way handoff.

Handoff permanently moves cold keys to the ordinary log. To bind this transition to the recovered foundation, the coordinator proposes a bridge entry

F=Bridge​(M,H⁡(M),VM).F=\textsc{Bridge}(M,H(M),V_{M}).

The bridge has an internal identifier and no client response. Ordinary Paxos phase one and choice preserve its exact metadata. Accepting it votes for the foundation entry without re-accepting referenced user writes. Bulk voters retain the bound bodies, with a survivor after at most ff crashes.

A replica cannot execute past FF until it validates the foundation and obtains all hash-checked bodies. Executing FF installs recovered cold state, imports chosen identifiers into ordinary deduplication, and atomically marks the replica migrated. Installation occurs once, preventing replay from overwriting later writes with an old foundation. Local bridge acceptance, mode hints, and body receipt cannot authorize migration.

After migration, all keys use the ordinary log in strict-prefix mode: reads wait for their relevant slot to execute, and write replies require actual execution. Direct acceptance certificates and cold admission stay disabled. Stale cold requests retain their identities when rerouted to the log. Stale control and proof messages cannot alter migrated state. Historical bodies support reconstruction but grant no authority.

Further failures.

Later leaders run ordinary phase one, preserve selected bridges, and resume prefix replay and body fetching without starting a separate cold history. A locally accepted but unselected bridge awaits phase-one resolution; acceptance alone cannot establish handoff. After migration, failures use ordinary-log and roster recovery.

A.4 Client and Replica Failure Details

Client failures.

Both ordering mechanisms retain full commands at replicas before voting. If a client fails before disseminating a proof, phase one preserves possibly chosen values from acceptance records; proof absence cannot rule out a choice.

Replica failures.

Ordinary writes can continue after nonmandatory replica failures if a majority and all required responders survive. Losing an ordinary read responder or a member of QbQ_{b} requires a higher roster ballot, even with a live leader. Old leases are fenced and replacement responders catch up before activation. The cold plane uses the recovery and handoff in § A.3; its fast quorum stays fixed throughout ballot bb, including changes of key round.

Payload and response recovery.

Replicas fetch hash-bound bodies and predecessor proofs from original holders. Transfers are idempotent and confer no vote or read authority. ColdDone requires the original command’s chosen evidence and, after migration, ordinary prefix execution. Retries retain original identifiers and complete at most once. Eligible writes may complete through certificates; executed replies require prefix execution at the planned completion replica.

A.5 Completion and Read-Execution Details

Early completion.

Ordinary certificates shorten evidence delivery to clients; the leader still orders commands. The cold path also removes this ordering hop for enabled, uncontended per-key instances. Both certificate paths require recoverable acceptance certificates before write completion. Write acknowledgements need no speculative execution of unchosen commands. Read results require valid read visibility.

Read execution.

Normal-mode reads beyond the applied prefix use chosen key values under the freshness, fixed-prefix, and lease conditions in § A.2, without speculative suffix execution. Broader certificate eligibility can hold more reads behind accepted writes that may already have completed elsewhere. Read races preserve visibility checks, so placement accounts for write-evidence delivery and read waiting.

The handoff boundary.

Bridge acceptance disables early client votes; ordered application installs the foundation and permanently enables strict-prefix execution. Reads cannot pass an unapplied bridge, and later writes cannot combine cold votes with ordinary acceptances. Later operations follow one recovered foundation and one ordinary executed prefix.

A.6 Routing and Delivery Optimizations

Ingress and direct admission.

The designated reply replica is implemented as a logical ingress. The planner chooses this ordinary write ingress using the modeled end-to-end write cost, rather than simply choosing the nearest replica. A designated completion owner, when usable, becomes the ingress for its key. The client can also submit the same write directly to the leader while retaining that ingress identity. Duplicate submissions are coalesced. A leader’s executed-result notification does not let the ingress acknowledge a write it has not itself executed. These routes change message arrival times, not certificate conditions.

Selective acceptance delivery.

Accepting replicas send ordinary votes to the leader and the learners selected to complete writes; eligible writes additionally generate client votes. Restricting recipients reduces traffic. It does not reduce the number or identity requirements of the votes a recipient must collect. Commit notices and repair messages let other replicas learn and execute the chosen history. Recipient selection is an optimization; delaying publication of a completion gate’s own vote until it has locally established coverage is a protocol rule.

Read races.

A client may send the same read to more than one authorized responder and use the first valid reply. Each responder independently checks its lease, catch-up state, and visibility predicate. Later replies do not create another logical completion. Racing requests cannot make an unsafe value visible.

Streams and body transfers.

Protocol messages, including recovery traffic, share one protocol stream per peer pair. Shared control/RTT RPCs are separate from these protocol streams. Fragments, retransmissions, and fetched bodies remain bound to their identifiers and hashes; receiving them alone neither chooses a value nor restores read authority.

A.7 Detailed Workload-Aware Planning

Inputs and decisions.

Let 𝒦\mathcal{K} be the key domain. From an independent profiling sample of NN offered requests, the system records

N⁡(k)=NR​(k)+NW​(k)N(k)=N^{R}(k)+N^{W}(k)

accesses to each observed key kk, where NR​(k)N^{R}(k) and NW​(k)N^{W}(k) are its sampled read and write counts. Observed keys are ordered by decreasing N⁡(k)N(k), with key identifier used only to break ties. If kjk_{j} is the key at popularity rank jj, its empirical probability is

pj=N⁡(kj)N.p_{j}=\frac{N(k_{j})}{N}.

The runtime retains the inverse mapping ρ⁡(kj)=j\rho(k_{j})=j. An unobserved key has no rank and always uses the ordinary log. Its direct-certificate eligibility depends on the selected reference or all-key policy.

Measured boundaries.

Let U=|{k:N⁡(k)>0}|U=|\{k:N(k)>0\}| be the number of observed keys and N¯=N/U\overline{N}=N/U their mean sampled count. The hot boundary is

η=|{k:N⁡(k)>N¯}|.\eta=|\{k:N(k)>\overline{N}\}|.

Thus ranks 0,…,η−10,\ldots,\eta-1 are hot. Integer implementation compares a key’s count with ⌊N/U⌋\lfloor N/U\rfloor, which is equivalent to the strict comparison above. Equal-frequency keys remain on the same side of the boundary. A uniform sample has η=0\eta=0. This is a fixed empirical classification rule, not an optimality claim or an online estimate that changes during execution.

The cold-path search starts with candidate cutoff η\eta. It computes cumulative request mass over the remaining observed ranks and adds boundaries at the first complete frequency group crossing each of the fractions 1/7,…,6/71/7,\ldots,6/7 of that mass. A boundary at the end of all observed keys is omitted, and coincident boundaries are merged. There are at most seven candidates. The selected cutoff τ≥η\tau\geq\eta may leave a non-hot ordinary region η≤ρ⁡(k)<τ\eta\leq\rho(k)<\tau. If the cold path is disabled, every key uses the ordinary log. Neither boundary depends on a numeric key identifier. The heat profile is hash-pinned, loaded before planning, and immutable across recovery; original keys, rather than their ranks, remain in commands.

For NcN_{c} clients, placement additionally uses directed delays dx​yd_{xy}, request rates, and write fraction ww. A plan π\pi selects leader ℓ\ell, read responders SS containing ℓ\ell, client read responders ri∈Sr_{i}\in S, write ingresses hih_{i}, completion owners, certificate eligibility, and an optional cold quorum QQ. A rank cutoff τ\tau assigns observed keys with ρ⁡(k)≥τ\rho(k)\geq\tau to the cold path.

The model groups popularity ranks into cohorts gg, with probability mass PgP_{g} and effective write rate λg\lambda_{g}:

Pg=∑j∈gpj,λg=λ​∑j∈gpj2Pg,P_{g}=\sum_{j\in g}p_{j},\qquad\lambda_{g}=\lambda\frac{\sum_{j\in g}p_{j}^{2}}{P_{g}},

where λ\lambda is the aggregate configured write rate per millisecond. This grouping approximates the per-key distribution. Ordinary candidate search uses configured client weights; the final combined screen averages over clients uniformly.

Ordinary write costs.

Let zv​(x)=dℓ​v+dv​xz_{v}(x)=d_{\ell v}+d_{vx} be the time for replica vv’s acceptance to reach recipient xx after leader propagation. If ordm\operatorname{ord}_{m} denotes the mmth smallest arrival time, the required evidence reaches xx at

Eπ(x)=max{ordm⁡{zv​(x):v∈R},maxs∈Szs(x)}.\begin{split}E_{\pi}(x)=\max\bigl\{&\operatorname{ord}_{m}\{z_{v}(x):v\in R\},\\ &\max_{s\in S}z_{s}(x)\bigr\}.\end{split} (2)

The two terms capture majority acceptance and coverage of every authorized read responder. A nearby responder can lower read delay while raising write-evidence time.

For client ii, the model accounts for forwarding and direct submission using

ai=min⁡{di​hi+dhi​ℓ,di​ℓ+1​ms}.a_{i}=\min\{d_{ih_{i}}+d_{h_{i}\ell},\ d_{i\ell}+1\,\mathrm{ms}\}.

Certificate and ingress-return costs are

TiC\displaystyle T_{i}^{C} =ai+Eπ​(i)+2​ms,\displaystyle=a_{i}+E_{\pi}(i)+2\,\mathrm{ms}, (3)
TiH\displaystyle T_{i}^{H} =max⁡{di​hi,ai+Eπ​(hi)}+dhi​i.\displaystyle=\max\{d_{ih_{i}},a_{i}+E_{\pi}(h_{i})\}+d_{h_{i}i}. (4)

An eligible command has modeled cost min⁡{TiC,TiH}\min\{T_{i}^{C},T_{i}^{H}\}; other commands use TiHT_{i}^{H}. A cohort may designate a completion owner, the replica returning its executed replies, in place of the default ingress. Ordinary candidate search also adds 11 ms to read-network costs and selected write costs. These are fixed heuristic offsets, not measured processing delays or required runtime timers. In particular, the direct-admission implementation sends immediately; the model’s 11 ms term is not an enforced delay.

Read waiting.

The interval between acceptance and evidence arrival at responder rr is approximated by

Hr=[Eπ​(r)−dℓ​r]+,[x]+=max⁡{x,0}.H_{r}=[E_{\pi}(r)-d_{\ell r}]_{+},\qquad[x]_{+}=\max\{x,0\}.

Let Ni​r=di​r+dr​iN_{ir}=d_{ir}+d_{ri} and λg​rf=λg​sg​r\lambda^{f}_{gr}=\lambda_{g}s_{gr}, where sg​rs_{gr} scales the rate of writes imposing read fences. It is one for certificate-eligible cohorts. Otherwise, it is zero at a designated completion owner, reflecting entries for which that owner gates publication of its vote; it is the estimated remote-write fraction at a leader without such an owner, and one at other responders. With 𝟏\mathbf{1} denoting an indicator, the exponential approximation gives the read cumulative distribution function (CDF):

Fi​g​rR​(t)=𝟏t≥Ni​r​exp⁡(−λg​rf​[Hr+Ni​r−t]+).F^{R}_{igr}(t)=\mathbf{1}_{t\geq N_{ir}}\exp\!\left(-\lambda^{f}_{gr}[H_{r}+N_{ir}-t]_{+}\right). (5)

The extra waiting time Wg​rW_{gr} has expectation

𝔼⁡[Wg​r]=Hr−1−e−λg​rf​Hrλg​rf,\mathbb{E}[W_{gr}]=H_{r}-\frac{1-e^{-\lambda^{f}_{gr}H_{r}}}{\lambda^{f}_{gr}},

with value zero when λg​rf=0\lambda^{f}_{gr}=0. This residual-wait expression is used in preliminary mean estimates. Broader certificate eligibility can lower write latency while increasing read waiting. For a planned race between responders rr and ss, the combined screen uses Fr​(t)+Fs​(t)−Fr​s​(t)F_{r}(t)+F_{s}(t)-F_{rs}(t), where Fr​sF_{rs} accounts for overlapping fencing intervals caused by the same writes.

Cold-path costs.

A cold write requires every member of QQ, so its uncontended cost for client ii is

TiF=maxq∈Q⁡(di​q+dq​i)+2​ms.T_{i}^{F}=\max_{q\in Q}(d_{iq}+d_{qi})+2\,\mathrm{ms}.

The conflict approximation uses VQ=maxi⁡TiF+200V_{Q}=\max_{i}T_{i}^{F}+200 ms and ρg=min⁡{1,λg​VQ}\rho_{g}=\min\{1,\lambda_{g}V_{Q}\}. Let AA be the majority leader–replica RTT, BB the largest leader–QQ RTT, and DD the largest client–replica RTT. The additional recovery-cost proxy is ΔQ=2​A+2​max⁡{A,B}+B+D+20\Delta_{Q}=2A+2\max\{A,B\}+B+D+20 ms. The cold-write CDF is

Fi​gW,cold​(t)=(1−ρg)​𝟏t≥TiF+ρg​𝟏t≥TiF+ΔQ.F^{W,\mathrm{cold}}_{ig}(t)={}(1-\rho_{g})\mathbf{1}_{t\geq T_{i}^{F}}+\rho_{g}\mathbf{1}_{t\geq T_{i}^{F}+\Delta_{Q}}. (6)

Cold reads select a nearby authorized member of QQ. Their waiting model replaces the fixed interval HrH_{r} in Equation 5 with a write-duration distribution BgB_{g}: each of the NcN_{c} clients contributes durations TjFT_{j}^{F} and TjF+ΔQT_{j}^{F}+\Delta_{Q} with weights (1−ρg)/Nc(1-\rho_{g})/N_{c} and ρg/Nc\rho_{g}/N_{c}. The exponent becomes −λg​𝔼​[(Bg+Ni​r−t)+]-\lambda_{g}\mathbb{E}[(B_{g}+N_{ir}-t)_{+}], capturing both uncontended and recovering writes.

Joint objective and search.

Let Fi​g,πRF^{R}_{ig,\pi} and Fi​g,πWF^{W}_{ig,\pi} be the modeled CDFs for cohort gg. The final screen combines cohort masses and uniform client weights:

Fπ​(t)=∑gPgNc​∑i[(1−w)​Fi​g,πR​(t)+w​Fi​g,πW​(t)].F_{\pi}(t)=\sum_{g}\frac{P_{g}}{N_{c}}\sum_{i}\bigl[(1-w)F^{R}_{ig,\pi}(t)+wF^{W}_{ig,\pi}(t)\bigr]. (7)

The implemented midpoint sum with h=0.25h=0.25 ms estimates the truncated mean

𝔼⁡[min⁡{T,1000​ms}].\mathbb{E}\!\left[\min\{T,1000\,\mathrm{ms}\}\right].

Quantiles are defined by the CDF and estimated with 3535 bisection iterations on [0,1000][0,1000] ms:

μ^π\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}_{\pi} =h​∑j=03999[1−Fπ​((j+12)​h)],\displaystyle=h\sum_{j=0}^{3999}[1-F_{\pi}((j+\tfrac{1}{2})h)], (8)
qπ​(u)\displaystyle q_{\pi}(u) =inf{t:Fπ​(t)≥u}.\displaystyle=\inf\{t:F_{\pi}(t)\geq u\}. (9)

This mixture evaluates overlapping read/write effects together; individual path savings are not added separately.

For memberships up to 1313 replicas, the ordinary search considers leader/responder combinations, chooses a nearby responder for each client, and compares ingress and completion assignments. An alternative stage selects a best-mean candidate allowing certificates for all ordinary keys. Above 1313 replicas, this all-key exploration is skipped; the inherited planner uses a bounded topology-derived base search and subsequent refinement. These are implementation search restrictions, not limits on the quorum rules. The cold stage ranks size-mm cold quorums by a workload-weighted combination of cold-read and uncontended-write cost, retains up to 6464 candidates, and searches the measured cutoff candidates defined above. This stage screens a coarse mean-gain proxy and nearby tail quantiles. Its tail search uses a 10,00010{,}000 ms upper bound, distinct from the 10001000 ms final comparison below. It prefers modeled 0.990.99-quantile improvement, breaking ties by mean gain; it can also disable the cold plane.

Candidate π1\pi_{1} is compared with reference plan π0\pi_{0}. The reference plan permits direct ordinary certificates only for observed keys with ρ⁡(k)≥η\rho(k)\geq\eta, whereas π1\pi_{1} permits them for all ordinary-path writes. Keys absent from the empirical profile remain on the ordinary path and use the conservative reference behavior unless the all-key policy is selected. Define Δ​μ=μ^π0−μ^π1\Delta\mu=\widehat{\mu}_{\pi_{0}}-\widehat{\mu}_{\pi_{1}} and Δ​q​(u)=qπ0​(u)−qπ1​(u)\Delta q(u)=q_{\pi_{0}}(u)-q_{\pi_{1}}(u). When the alternative enables all-key certificates, select it when

Δ​μ>ε∧minu∈𝒰⁡Δ​q​(u)≥−γ​Δ​μ,\Delta\mu>\varepsilon\quad\land\quad\min_{u\in\mathcal{U}}\Delta q(u)\geq-\gamma\Delta\mu, (10)

where the current heuristic uses ε=0.05\varepsilon=0.05 ms, γ=5\gamma=5, and 𝒰={0.9898,0.9900,0.9902}\mathcal{U}=\{0.9898,0.9900,0.9902\}. The selected plan is fixed before normal operation, and its roles become active through the lease, promise, and catch-up transitions in § 4.4.

Scope of the model.

The numerical grid, truncation bounds, and fixed offsets above are performance heuristics. They do not grant votes, leases, or read authority, and the selection test does not guarantee an improvement in measured mean or tail latency. The rank aggregation and moment-expansion boundaries in the implementation control numerical approximation independently of hot membership and candidate cold cutoffs. The profile counts both reads and writes; the model uses a configured write fraction to estimate per-key write pressure rather than inferring a separate write fraction for every key. A workload change can therefore make a fixed plan inefficient without changing its safety conditions.

Appendix E Protocol Counterexamples

E.1 Tentative Metadata Authorizes an Unsafe Pruning Decision

Audit question.

Is the metadata used to justify pruning already final? EPaxos Revisited [75] uses sequence numbers and dependencies to prune commands that appear to execute after the current instance. A tentative PREACCEPTED tuple can differ from the tuple fixed by COMMIT, so using it to authorize a cutoff can expose an incorrect order.

Setup.

Three replicas r0,r1,r2r_{0},r_{1},r_{2} run EPaxos with dependency pruning enabled. Conflicting commands XX and YY originate at r0r_{0} and r2r_{2}, respectively. No replica fails; selected PREACCEPT and COMMIT messages are delayed.

Counterexample.

In Figure 11, command XX first commits at r0r_{0} with no dependencies. Command YY subsequently commits with a dependency on XX, so r0r_{0} executes XX before YY. At r2r_{2}, however, a delayed PREACCEPT for XX arrives only after YY has committed. The tentative local tuple gives XX a higher sequence number and a dependency on YY. If the pruning rule treats that tentative tuple as final evidence, it removes XX from YY’s dependency chain and permits r2r_{2} to execute YY first. The later COMMIT for XX overwrites the tentative tuple, but it arrives too late to undo the order already exposed at r2r_{2}. Replica r2r_{2} subsequently executes XX, reversing r0r_{0}’s order and violating execution consistency.

E.2 Pruning a Committed Node Can Hide an Earlier Dependency

Audit question.

Does finality of the pruned node justify discarding its entire dependency branch in EPaxos Revisited [75]? Unlike § E.1, this counterexample already requires the pruned node to be committed.

Setup.

Three replicas originate conflicting commands CC, AA, and BB at owners r0r_{0}, r1r_{1}, and r2r_{2}, respectively. Dependency pruning is enabled; no replica fails and no recovery occurs.

Counterexample.

Normal-path processing and fast decisions produce the tuples shown in Figure 12. The full committed graph is one SCC. Commands CC and AA tie at sequence 1, and the replica-ID tie-breaker places CC before AA; BB has sequence 2. Replica r0r_{0} selects BB as its execution root and executes C,A,BC,A,B. Replica r1r_{1}, however, learns the committed BB tuple while executing AA. The reciprocal dependency and strict sequence inequality allow it to prune BB. The cutoff hides CC, whose final tuple is not yet known locally. It executes AA, later learns CC, and executes CC, reversing the order of the conflicting pair A,CA,C and violating execution consistency despite the pruned node’s committed metadata.

E.3 Early Reads Expose a Value Missing from the Leader’s Read View

One of the authors had identified this issue before the agent but the agent received no hint about it and found it independently.

Audit question.

Does every read path respect a value already exposed by an early read, even before the leader commits that write? Bodega’s main algorithm [29, §3.2.2 and Fig. 7] permits a non-leader responder to return an accepted value after collecting majority accept notifications (lines 38–39), but directs a stable leader to return the last committed value (line 36).

Setup.

Three replicas L,A,BL,A,B tolerate one failure; the trace itself has no failures. The fixed ballot and roster designate LL as leader and AA as the responder for key kk, initially absent. The roster is installed, the leader is prepared, and read-serving replicas hold valid majority-backed leases with catch-up thresholds zero. Early accept is enabled. No lease expiration or roster change occurs.

Counterexample.

As shown in Figure 13, Writer WW invokes w=Write​(k,7)w=\textsc{Write}(k,7), which LL proposes at log slot zero after preparation. All three replicas accept ww. The accept replies from AA and BB to LL remain delayed, so the leader cannot commit the write. AA collects accept notifications from the majority {L,B}\{L,B\}. Reader RR then invokes r1=Read​(k)r_{1}=\textsc{Read}(k). At AA, the notifications authorize an early reply with 77 while the write remains uncommitted locally. After receiving that result, RR invokes r2=Read​(k)r_{2}=\textsc{Read}(k). When this read reaches LL, its stable-leader read path uses the committed state, which is still empty, and returns absence. The second read can reach the leader after the client unhold timeout while its response from AA is delayed. The write remains pending throughout.

E.4 Duplicate Writes from Client Retries

Audit question.

Can retrying a timed-out write cause the same client operation to take effect twice? In Bodega [29], the client’s timeout retry path assigns a new request identifier to each write attempt. The server treats the original request and its retry as separate writes, so both can execute.

Setup.

Two clients access a key xx, initially 00, through a leader in a three-replica deployment. Client C1C_{1} invokes W1=Write​(x,1)W_{1}=\textsc{Write}(x,1) with timeout retries enabled. The original request and its retries represent this single write and should take effect only once. The reply to the first attempt is delayed beyond the client timeout; all reads return committed values.

Counterexample.

As shown in Figure 14, the first attempt of W1W_{1}, with request identifier uu, sets x=1x=1, but its reply is delayed. Client C2C_{2} reads xx and obtains 11, then completes W2=Write​(x,2)W_{2}=\textsc{Write}(x,2). After timing out, C1C_{1} resubmits Write(x,1)(x,1) with a new identifier u′≠uu^{\prime}\neq u. The server executes the retry, overwriting 22 with 11, and its reply completes C1C_{1}’s write. A subsequent read by C2C_{2} returns 11. The first read requires W1W_{1} to take effect before W2W_{2}. If both attempts belong to the same write W1W_{1}, there is no additional write after W2W_{2}, so the final read must return 22. Returning 11 therefore violates linearizability for these client operations.

Appendix F Comparison with AI-Driven Discovery Approaches

Table 4compares AI-greement with prior AI-based work that generates algorithms or protocols automatically. AI-driven discovery has already produced new algorithms, but mostly for single-node code or for policies that a simulator can score. For distributed systems, prior AI work either synthesizes verified implementations of a fixed specification, finds bugs in existing protocols, learns small protocols checked only for a bounded number of processes, without a performance objective, or assists humans in designing protocols proved by hand.

To compare discovery procedures, we adopt the nomenclature of SkyDiscover [44], which decomposes AI-driven discovery into four components, and use it to describe all systems in Table 5, including AI-greement. A context builder assembles the prompt from the problem and from earlier solutions, a solution generator produces candidates, an evaluator scores them (by simulation, benchmarking, testing, or proof checking), and a solution selector decides which earlier solutions guide the next iteration. AI-greement follows the same loop. It differs in three ways: its context is a curated consensus knowledge base rather than prior programs alone, its evaluator stages benchmarks, fault injection, and Lean proofs so that cheaper checks reject candidates first, and its selector is the agent itself, which chooses a parent from recorded lessons rather than from a population by a fixed rule.

The selectors of FunSearch, AlphaEvolve, ADRS, and SkyDiscover come from evolutionary computation and operate on a population of candidates. In the island model, the population is split into subpopulations (islands) that evolve independently: each new candidate is built from parents of a single island, and islands occasionally exchange their best candidates or are reseeded from stronger ones, which keeps the search from converging prematurely on one line of solutions. MAP-Elites preserves diversity differently, by keeping the best candidate for each cell of a grid of solution features, such as program length or behavior. None of the other systems maintains such a population: AlphaDev and GGMS select by tree search, IDS by a coordinator, and Glia and AI-greement by the agent’s own judgment.

Three challenges set consensus apart from the problems that AI-driven discovery has addressed so far. (C1) Performance conflicts with correctness: the cheapest way to reduce latency is to shrink a quorum or skip a round, which breaks agreement, so a performance score alone steers the search toward incorrect protocols. (C2) Tests cannot establish correctness: safety violations arise in rare interleavings of messages, failures, and recovery that benchmarks seldom reach, so safety requires a proof, and a proof is only as good as its specification. (C3) Evaluation is expensive: each candidate requires an implementation, a geo-distributed benchmark, fault injection, and a proof attempt, which takes minutes to hours rather than seconds, so thousands of candidates cannot be evaluated. Table 6 shows which of these challenges prior work faces. In classical algorithms and in distributed-systems policies, every candidate is either valid by construction or checked exactly and cheaply, so none of the three arises. The few AI-driven approaches to distributed protocols sidestep them by dropping the performance objective, fixing the specification, or restricting the search to three or four processes.
